newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices resume rally on U.S. stock shortfall.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices resume rally on U.S. stock shortfall.

text.p: World oil prices edged upwards on Wednesday, but still remained $2 off their recent highs, on growing concern about low U.S. stocks of heating oil in addition to continuing military tension in the Gulf.
November futures for benchmark Brent Blend crude oil rose 49 cents to $22.20 per barrel by 1642 GMT, still $2 below last week's post-Gulf War high.

"The market has temporarily put aside its fear of hostility in Iraq and is once again focusing on low heating oil inventories," said Peter Bogin, oil analyst at Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris.

Heating oil stocks in the United States, the world's biggest oil consumer, were almost a third lower than this time last year, according to data released by the American Petroleum Institute on Tuesday night.

"If the inventory situation improves, prices will come off. But if it does not improve over the next month or two, prices could stay at this level for the rest of the year and into next year," Bogin said.

Brent futures hit a post-Gulf War high of $24.39 per barrel last week after Baghdad moved troops into Iraq's northern Kurd-controlled region, prompting U.S. air strikes and a massive mobilisation of U.S. firepower in the region.
But prices deflated over the weekend as the war of words between Iraq and the United States eased.
"The political premium has come out of the market for the moment," said Bogin. "But if things heat up in the Middle East again, that premium will come back."
The latest Gulf crisis was merely another reason to buy in an already bullish market.
So far this year, Brent futures have averaged $19.00 per barrel, $3.00 above 1995. Bogin said consumers would soon begin to feel the impact of higher prices, if they have not already.

"In Europe there is so much of a tax cushion that consumers are protected from oil price rises, but heating oil prices are astoundingly high compared to last year. People will start to notice it when they pay their bills in the fourth quarter," Bogin said.
On Wednesday, the price of heating oil on European cargo markets was 40 percent above this time last year $225 per tonne.
The higher cost of oil imports played a major part in the widening of the U.S. trade deficit in July, which surged to its highest level in eight years, the U.S. Commerce Department said on Wednesday.
The unexpected news sent the dollar tumbling against the other major currencies, falling below 110 yen and 1.51 marks, Wall Street dealers said.
